## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all the colors of the visible spectrum, but when it enters Earth's atmosphere it collides with the tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These molecules scatter the incoming light in all directions through a process called **Rayleigh scattering**, and they do so much more effectively for shorter wavelengths. As a result, the blue and violet portions of sunlight are scattered across the entire sky, so when you look up (away from the Sun directly), you see this diffuse blue light arriving from every direction. The sky appears blue rather than violet because our eyes are more sensitive to blue, the Sun emits more blue than violet, and some violet light is absorbed higher in the atmosphere.

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the **fourth power** of the wavelength:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This strong dependence means shorter wavelengths scatter dramatically more than longer ones. For example, blue light (~450 nm) scatters roughly **6 times** more intensely than red light (~700 nm), which is the physical basis for the blue sky (and, at sunset, the reddening of the Sun as blue light has been scattered away along the longer path through the atmosphere).

So the combination we perceive is blue.
